claim: Artificial skin-stretch increases the predictive grip force modulation in anticipation of the load force.
source: We found that artificial skin-stretch increases the predictive grip force modulation in anticipation of the load force.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data from Experiment 1 showing increased grip force modulation with skin-stretch.

claim: Skin-stretch causes an immediate illusion of touching a harder object that does not depend on the gradual development of the predictive modulation of grip force.
source: Moreover, the stretch causes an immediate illusion of touching a harder object that does not depend on the gradual development of the predictive modulation of grip force.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 comparing single-probe and free-exploration groups.

claim: Perception of the impedance of objects is based on the integration of motion and force signals sensed during contact with the environment.
source: Since we do not possess sensors for mechanical impedance, the perception of the impedance of objects, such as their stiffness, damping, and inertia, is based on the integration of motion and force signals, which are sensed during contact with the environment (Jones and Hunter, 1993; Nisky et al., 2008; Kuschel et al., 2010; Nisky et al., 2010; Gurari et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research establishing this principle.

claim: Individuals with impaired tactile sensitivity are deprived of important information required for planning and controlling object manipulation.
source: Individuals with impaired tactile sensitivity are deprived of important information required for planning and controlling object manipulation, such as the magnitude and direction of contact forces, the shape of contact surfaces, and friction (Johansson and Flanagan, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on tactile sensitivity and object manipulation.

claim: The unique role of tactile information in the discrimination of subtle differences in softness has been identified using anesthesia and passive stimulation via robots.
source: Using anesthesia and passive stimulation via robots, the unique role of tactile information in the discrimination of subtle differences in softness has been identified (Srinivasan and LaMotte, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research using anesthesia and robotic stimulation.

claim: Passive or anesthetized touch is different from active touch with intact tactile sensing.
source: However, passive or anesthetized touch is different from active touch with intact tactile sensing (Gwilliam et al., 2014), and the combination of kinesthetic and tactile information in perception and action is still poorly understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research comparing passive/anesthetized and active touch.

claim: Tactor-induced skin-stretch has successfully conveyed direction information in sensory substitution studies.
source: For example, tactor-induced skin-stretch has successfully conveyed direction information (Gleeson et al., 2009), navigation cues (Quek et al., 2015a) and stiffness information (Schorr et al., 2015) in sensory substitution studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on skin-stretch for direction information.

claim: Adding artificial skin-stretch to kinesthetic force has been shown to augment the perceived friction.
source: Additionally, adding artificial skin-stretch to kinesthetic force has been shown to augment the perceived friction (Provancher and Sylvester, 2009) and perceived stiffness (Quek et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on skin-stretch and perceived friction.

claim: Stretching the skin more than it would be during natural interactions causes the object to feel stiffer than it really is.
source: Meaning, stretching the skin more than it would be during natural interactions, causes the object to feel stiffer than it really is.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from previous studies cited in the preceding sentence about augmented perceived stiffness.

claim: Previous studies do not provide information about the time-course of the formation of perceptual illusions caused by skin-stretch.
source: These studies, however, do not provide any information about the time-course of the formation of the perceptual illusions caused by the skin-stretch, or about the role of skin-stretch in grip force control.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in the literature based on review of previous studies.

claim: Three known components contribute to grip force: a predictive feedforward component (baseline grip force and modulation in anticipation of load force) and a reactive feedback component that responds to slippage.
source: When interacting with an object, three known components contribute to our grip force: a predictive feedforward component, which consists of a baseline grip force and a modulation of grip force in anticipation of the load force; and a reactive feedback component that responds to slippage.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations in the following sentences.

claim: Feedforward control is used to adjust grip force in accordance with the expected slipperiness and weight of the object.
source: Feedforward control is used to adjust our grip force in accordance with the expected slipperiness and weight (or load force) of the object (Flanagan and Wing, 1990; Flanagan and Wing, 1997; Flanagan et al., 2003; Danion and Sarlegna, 2007; Danion et al., 2009; Leib et al., 2015; Leib et al., 2018; White et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research on feedforward grip force control.

claim: Grip force adjustment often starts in anticipation to the change in load force.
source: This adjustment often starts in anticipation to the change in load force (Forssberg et al., 1992), and several recent studies revealed that the intended peak grip force can be predicted from the grip force and the rate of its change at the time of initial contact with the object (White et al., 2011; Kuling et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on anticipatory grip force adjustment.

claim: Baseline grip force is maintained to create a safety margin and is increased when one experiences uncertainty regarding the load force.
source: Baseline grip force is maintained to create a safety margin, and is increased when one experiences uncertainty regarding the load force (Gibo et al., 2013; Hadjiosif and Smith, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on baseline grip force and uncertainty.

claim: Predictive modulation is calculated based on an internal representation of the object dynamics, which is learned by the nervous system.
source: Predictive modulation is calculated based on an internal representation of the object dynamics, which is learned by the nervous system (Johansson and Cole, 1992; Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994; Kawato, 1999; Davidson and Wolpert, 2004) and is updated during repeated interactions (Donchin et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research on internal representations and motor learning.

claim: If cutaneous receptors detect slippage, the grip force is increased through rapid feedback control.
source: Finally, if cutaneous receptors detect that slippage is occurring, the grip force is increased through rapid feedback control (Kandel, 2000; Johansson and Flanagan, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on feedback control of grip force.

claim: Tactile information has been shown to be necessary for scaling the grip force strength.
source: Tactile information can be completely removed by digital anesthesia, and by doing so, has been shown to be necessary for scaling the grip force strength.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from studies using digital anesthesia, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: The left supplementary motor area is involved in the scaling of grip force.
source: Additionally, a recent rTMS study suggested that the left supplementary motor area, known to be involved in processing tactile information (Romo et al., 1993; Kim et al., 2015), is involved in the scaling of grip force (White et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research using rTMS and studies on the supplementary motor area.

claim: The timing of grip force can be predictively regulated by kinesthetic information alone.
source: The timing, on the other hand, can be predictively regulated by kinesthetic information alone (Nowak et al., 2001; Witney et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on kinesthetic control of grip force timing.

claim: In the complete absence of force information, grip force is not modulated in accordance with the load force, and the baseline grip force is increased to prevent slippage.
source: In the complete absence of force information, grip force is not modulated in accordance with the load force, and the baseline grip force is increased to prevent slippage (Gibo et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on grip force in the absence of force information.

claim: Two recent studies using skin-stretch technology yielded conflicting results regarding the effects of skin-stretch on grip force, reporting an increased and unchanged mean grip force, respectively.
source: Two recent studies using this technology yielded conflicting results regarding the effects of skin-stretch on grip force, reporting an increased (Quek et al., 2015a) and unchanged (Quek et al., 2015b) mean grip force, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two previous studies with conflicting results.

claim: It is unknown how artificial skin-stretch affects the predictive modulation of grip force in anticipation of load force.
source: However, it is unknown how artificial skin-stretch affects the predictive modulation of grip force in anticipation of load force.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in the literature based on review of previous studies.

claim: There are many examples of the dissociation of sensory information processing for perception and action during grasping and lifting of objects.
source: There are many examples of the dissociation of sensory information processing for perception and action during grasping (Aglioti et al., 1995; Haffenden et al., 2001) and lifting of objects (Flanagan and Beltzner, 2000; Bringoux et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research on perception-action dissociation.

claim: The size-weight illusion affects the scaling of grip force in the first trials of a lifting task, but with repeated lifting movements the motor effect fades away, while the perceptual illusion persists.
source: For example, the size-weight illusion affects the scaling of grip force in the first trials of a lifting task, but with repeated lifting movements the motor effect fades away, while the perceptual illusion persists (Flanagan and Beltzner, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on the size-weight illusion.

claim: During interactions with linear elastic force fields, a delay in the force feedback produces the illusion of touching a softer spring, but the participants' grip force is predictively adjusted to the correct stiffness level and timing.
source: During interactions with linear elastic force fields, a delay in the force feedback produces the illusion of touching a softer spring, but the participants' grip force is predictively adjusted to the correct stiffness level and timing (Leib et al., 2015; Leib et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on delayed force feedback.

claim: Introducing a delay in visual feedback led to a persistent alteration of grip force control due to an illusory change in object dynamics.
source: Conversely, introducing a delay in visual feedback led to a persistent alteration of grip force control due to an illusory change in object dynamics (Sarlegna et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on delayed visual feedback.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants (N = 10) sat in front of a virtual reality setup and interacted with virtual elastic force fields created by a haptic device.
source: Participants (N = 10) sat in front of a virtual reality setup and interacted with virtual elastic force fields which were created by a haptic device.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup and procedure in Experiment 1.

claim: The standard force field had a constant stiffness value of 85 N/m.
source: When interacting with the standard force field, in addition to the load force feedback, which had a constant stiffness value of 85 N/m, the skin of the thumb and index finger was stretched using a skin-stretch device (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental parameters in Experiment 1.

claim: The stiffness of the comparison force field was chosen to be one of three different stiffness values (40, 85, and 130 N/m).
source: The stiffness of the comparison force field in each trial was chosen to be one of three different stiffness values (40, 85, and 130 N/m).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental parameters in Experiment 1.

claim: The gain of the skin-stretch stimulation in each trial was chosen from four possible values (0, 33, 66, and 100 mm/m).
source: The gain of the skin-stretch stimulation (i.e. the amount of skin-stretch relative to the penetration depth) in each trial was chosen from four possible values (0, 33, 66, and 100 mm/m).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental parameters in Experiment 1.

claim: Participants made eight discrete movements into each of the two force fields in each trial.
source: In each trial, participants made eight discrete movements into each of the two force fields.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure in Experiment 1.

claim: Despite the skin-stretch stimulation, participants maintained the grip force-load force modulation.
source: These trajectories clearly show that despite the skin-stretch stimulation, participants maintained the grip force-load force modulation.
evidence: This claim is based on visual examination of grip force trajectories shown in Figure 2.

claim: During probes with high levels of tactor displacement gain, the grip force signals have a double peak pattern.
source: In Figure 2c and d, we can see that during probes with high levels of tactor displacement gain, the grip force signals have a double peak pattern.
evidence: This claim is based on visual examination of grip force trajectories shown in Figure 2c and d.

claim: Repeated interactions with the force field led to an increase in the predictive grip force control in the event of large tactor displacement gains (66 and 100 mm/m).
source: Figure 2c and d also show that in the event of large tactor displacement gains (66 and 100 mm/m), repeated interactions with the force field led to an increase in the predictive grip force control.
evidence: This claim is based on visual examination of grip force trajectories shown in Figure 2c and d.

claim: The observed decrease in peak grip force-peak load force ratio is consistent with previous results reported in the literature.
source: This observed decrease is consistent with previous results reported in the literature (Leib et al., 2015; Leib et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim compares the current findings to previous research cited.

claim: Repeated interactions with the elastic force field may have improved participants' certainty about the internal representation of the force field, allowing them to lower their grip force.
source: A likely cause is that repeated interactions with the elastic force field may have improved participants' certainty about the internal representation of the force field, allowing them to lower their grip force.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on inference.

claim: Participants applied more grip force per amount of kinesthetic load force when interacting with force fields with higher levels of tactor displacement gain.
source: That is, participants applied more grip force per amount of kinesthetic load force when interacting with force fields with higher levels of tactor displacement gain.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the peak grip force-peak load force ratio shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The gentle increase in the second probing movement can be explained by the fact that participants had already been exposed to the skin-stretch stimulus in the first movement, and could therefore predict the stimulus.
source: The gentle increase in the second probing movement can be explained by the fact that participants had already been exposed to the skin-stretch stimulus in the first movement, and could therefore predict the stimulus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on inference.

claim: With repeated interactions, the participants continued to build up the increase in the anticipatory control of their applied grip force.
source: The steep increase in the seventh probing movement suggests that with repeated interactions, the participants continued to build up the increase in the anticipatory control of their applied grip force.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on inference from the data.

claim: The intercept of the grip force-load force regression is close to the baseline grip force.
source: The intercept of this regression is close to the baseline grip force; i.e. the amount of grip force that was applied by the participants when no external load force was applied by the haptic device.
evidence: This is a methodological explanation based on established analysis techniques.

claim: The slope of the grip force-load force regression represents the modulation of the grip force in anticipation of the load force.
source: The slope of the regression represents the modulation of the grip force in anticipation of the load force, that is, the amount of change in the grip force per change in the load force during the interaction with the force field.
evidence: This is a methodological explanation based on established analysis techniques.

claim: Prior works that studied interaction with elastic objects linked the slope to both the slip ratio and the anticipated load force.
source: Prior works that studied interaction with elastic objects linked the slope to both the slip ratio and the anticipated load force (Flanagan and Wing, 1990; Leib et al., 2015; Leib et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on grip force-load force relationships.

claim: The decrease in intercept indicates that participants became more confident about their estimation of the stiffness of the elastic force fields and the slipperiness of the contact.
source: As the intercept represents the applied safety margin, this decrease indicates that participants became more confident about their estimation of the stiffness of the elastic force fields and the slipperiness of the contact.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on inference.

claim: The lack of change in the slope suggests that there was little or no change in the represented stiffness or slip ratio.
source: The lack of change in the slope suggests that there was little or no change in the represented stiffness or slip ratio.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on inference.

claim: The addition of the artificial skin-stretch increased the participants' uncertainty about their internal representation of the elastic force fields.
source: This suggests that the addition of the artificial skin-stretch increased the participants' uncertainty about their internal representation of the elastic force fields.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on inference from the increased intercept.

claim: Following repeated exposure to the artificial skin-stretch stimulation, the participants either increased their estimation of the expected force or of the slipperiness of the device.
source: This suggests that following repeated exposure to the artificial skin-stretch stimulation, the participants either increased their estimation of the expected force (likely due to the increase in the representation of the stiffness of the force field) or of the slipperiness of the device.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on inference from the increased slope.

claim: The slope values are small with respect to previous studies because the device only measures a downscaled version of the grip force.
source: It is important to mention that the slope values are small with respect to previous studies (Flanagan and Wing, 1990; Leib et al., 2015) as our device only measures a downscaled version of the grip force (see methods and Appendix 2 for more information).
evidence: This is an explanation of the experimental results based on the device characteristics.

claim: In the first probing movement, the baseline grip force values of all the tactor displacement gains are similar.
source: In the first probing movement, the baseline grip force values of all the tactor displacement gains are similar.
evidence: This claim is based on visual examination of data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Already in the second movement a difference between the grip force baseline values of the different tactor displacement gains can be observed.
source: However, already in the second movement a difference between the grip force baseline values of the different tactor displacement gains can be observed.
evidence: This claim is based on visual examination of data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Due to the additional tactile stimulation, the grip force baseline increased in accordance to the amount of stretch immediately following the first probing movement.
source: Meaning, due to the additional tactile stimulation, the grip force baseline increased in accordance to the amount of stretch immediately following the first probing movement.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on the data analysis.

claim: The intended peak grip force was similar between the different tactor displacement gains in the first probing movement.
source: Here too, the intended peak grip force was similar between the different tactor displacement gains in the first probing movement.
evidence: This claim is based on visual examination of data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The gradual change in grip force modulation culminates after four probing movements.
source: This analysis enables us to pinpoint the time-course of the change with greater precision than the stretch-catch probe analysis; calculating the grip force modulation showed that the gradual change culminates after four probing movements.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on the data analysis.

claim: Following exposure to high levels of artificial skin-stretch participants immediately increased their safety margin and maintained it even after many interactions.
source: To summarize, we found that following exposure to high levels of artificial skin-stretch participants immediately increased their safety margin and maintained it even after many interactions.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from Experiment 1.

claim: Participants increased the predictive grip force modulation in anticipation of the load force, and this increase developed gradually with subsequent probing interactions with the same elastic force field.
source: They also increased the predictive grip force modulation in anticipation of the load force. This increase developed gradually with subsequent probing interactions with the same elastic force field.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from Experiment 1.

claim: Previous studies showed that when participants freely explored the stiffness of elastic force fields, adding artificial skin-stretch caused an increase in the perceived stiffness.
source: Previous studies (Quek et al., 2013; Quek et al., 2014) showed that when participants freely explored (used as many probing movements as they wished) the stiffness of elastic force fields, adding artificial skin-stretch caused an increase in the perceived stiffness.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on skin-stretch and perceived stiffness.

claim: The perceptual augmentation of stiffness was found to be linearly related to the tactor displacement gain.
source: Moreover, they found this perceptual augmentation to be linearly related to the tactor displacement gain (that is, the amount of skin-stretch per movement).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on skin-stretch and perceived stiffness.

claim: In Experiment 2, participants (N = 20) probed pairs of elastic force fields and determined which one had a higher level of stiffness.
source: Participants (N = 20) probed pairs of elastic force fields and determined which one had a higher level of stiffness.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure in Experiment 2.

claim: The standard force field in Experiment 2 had a constant stiffness value (85 N/m), and was augmented by one of four different tactor displacement gains (0, 33, 66, and 100 mm/m).
source: The standard force field had a constant stiffness value (85 N/m), and was augmented by one of four different tactor displacement gains (0, 33, 66, and 100 mm/m).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental parameters in Experiment 2.

claim: The stiffness of the comparison force field in Experiment 2 was chosen from a range of ten values, evenly spaced between 40–130 N/m.
source: The stiffness of the comparison force field was chosen from a range of ten values, evenly spaced between 40–130 N/m.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental parameters in Experiment 2.

claim: The participants in Experiment 2 were divided into two groups: Group 1 (N = 10) could probe each force field only once, and Group 2 (N = 10) used free exploration.
source: The participants were divided into two groups: Group 1 (N = 10) could probe each force field only once, and Group 2 (N = 10) used free exploration, meaning they could probe each force field as many times as they desired.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design in Experiment 2.

claim: Adding artificial skin-stretch to kinesthetic load force caused participants to overestimate the stiffness of the standard force field.
source: Adding artificial skin-stretch to kinesthetic load force caused participants to overestimate the stiffness of the standard force field.
evidence: This is a primary finding from Experiment 2 based on psychometric curve analysis.

claim: The augmentation in the perceived stiffness increased linearly as a function of the tactor displacement gain in both groups.
source: Our results show that the augmentation in the perceived stiffness increased linearly as a function of the tactor displacement gain in both groups.
evidence: This is a primary finding from Experiment 2 based on psychometric curve analysis.

claim: Artificial skin-stretch caused the illusion of touching a harder object, that is, overestimation of the perceived stiffness.
source: As shown in the psychometric curves, in trials lacking artificial skin-stretch (tactor displacement gain of 0 mm/m), the Point of Subjective Equality (PSE, a measure of bias in the perceived stiffness) was close to zero, and the slope of the psychometric curve was steep, indicating that the participant could accurately distinguish between the stiffness levels of the two force fields. Stretching the finger-pad skin of these participants during their interactions with the standard force field led to a rightward shift of the psychometric curves representing these trials, and a positive PSE, indicating that these participants overestimated the stiffness of the standard force field.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of psychometric curves shown in Figure 7.

claim: Stretching the finger-pad skin did not affect the stiffness discrimination ability.
source: These shifts of the PSE values occurred without practically any change in the slopes of the psychometric curve, indicating that stretching the finger-pad skin did not affect the stiffness discrimination ability.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of psychometric curves showing no change in slope.

claim: The increase in the average perceived stiffness for a gain of 100 mm/m in Group 1 was 30.73 N/m with a standard error of 2.26 N/m (35% of the kinesthetic stiffness level).
source: The increase in the average perceived stiffness for a gain of 100 mm/m was 30.73 N/m with a standard error of 2.26 N/m (35% of the kinesthetic stiffness level).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the statistical analysis of Group 1 data.

claim: The increase in the average perceived stiffness for a gain of 100 mm/m in Group 2 was 39.10 N/m with a standard error of 1.87 N/m (47% of the kinesthetic stiffness level).
source: The increase in the average perceived stiffness for a gain of 100 mm/m was 39.10 N/m with a standard error of 1.87 N/m (47% of the kinesthetic stiffness level).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the statistical analysis of Group 2 data.

claim: One participant in Group 2 showed the opposite trend in perceived stiffness because she was aware of the applied skin-stretch and tried to resist its effect.
source: The only participant who showed the opposite trend in perceived stiffness (that is, a decrease in the perceived stiffness due to the skin-stretch) reported that she was aware of the applied skin-stretch, and tried to resist its effect by responding the opposite to what she felt.
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from participant self-report.

claim: The added tactile stimulation did not impair the discrimination accuracy.
source: Based on this finding from the results of both groups, we therefore conclude that the added tactile stimulation did not impair the discrimination accuracy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the JND analysis in both groups.

claim: A direct comparison between the two groups revealed no differences in the bias in stiffness perception (PSE) or in the discrimination sensitivity (JND).
source: A direct comparison between the two groups revealed no differences in the bias in stiffness perception (as quantified by the PSE) or in the discrimination sensitivity (as quantified by the JND) of the two groups.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical comparison between the two groups.

claim: The perceptual illusion was formed immediately, after a single probing movement into the force field, and before the increase in the predictive modulation of grip force in anticipation of load force was formed.
source: We can therefore conclude that the perceptual illusion was formed immediately, after a single probing movement into the force field, and before the increase in the predictive modulation of grip force in anticipation of load force that we identified in Experiment 1 was formed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the results of the two groups in Experiment 2 with findings from Experiment 1.

claim: When high tactor displacement gains were applied, there was a rising trend in the magnitude of the applied grip force as the participant made subsequent probing movements.
source: Importantly, Figure 8 also shows that when high tactor displacement gains were applied, there was a rising trend in the magnitude of the applied grip force as the participant made subsequent probing movements.
evidence: This claim is based on visual examination of grip force trajectories shown in Figure 8.

claim: The increase in grip force in the first probing movement was a result of the reactive grip force response.
source: This was an unexpected result as participants could not predict the tactor displacement gain value in their first interaction with the force field. We therefore posit that this increase in grip force was a result of the reactive grip force response (see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the unexpected result based on inference and reference to additional analysis in Appendix 1.

claim: Adding artificial skin-stretch increases the perceived stiffness linearly with the tactor displacement gain.
source: To conclude, in this experiment, we reproduced the results that adding artificial skin-stretch increases the perceived stiffness (i.e. caused the illusion of touching a harder object) linearly with the tactor displacement gain.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from Experiment 2.

claim: The perceptual effect of skin-stretch was formed immediately upon the exposure to the skin-stretch stimulus.
source: We investigated the timescale of the formation of the perceptual effect and found that it was formed immediately upon the exposure to the skin-stretch stimulus.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from Experiment 2.

claim: The skin-stretch led to an increase in the overall grip force that developed with subsequent probing interactions with the same elastic force field.
source: This analysis confirmed that, here too, the skin-stretch led to an increase in the overall grip force that developed with subsequent probing interactions with the same elastic force field.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from Experiment 2.

claim: Artificial skin-stretch affected the prediction of the load force applied by the object, and consequentially led to a gradual increase in the predictive modulation of grip force in anticipation of the load force.
source: Our results suggest that artificial skin-stretch also affected the prediction of the load force applied by the object, and consequentially led to a gradual increase in the predictive modulation of grip force in anticipation of the load force.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: The perceptual illusion was formed immediately upon first contact with the object, and did not depend on the slower development of the predictive control of grip force.
source: Additionally, we discovered that the perceptual illusion was formed immediately upon first contact with the object, and did not depend on the slower development of the predictive control of grip force.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: Previous studies focused on patients with impairments or used digital anesthesia, and concluded that impaired cutaneous feedback increased the overall grip force, but did not affect the modulation of grip force in anticipation of load force.
source: Many of these studies focused on patients with impairments (Nowak and Hermsdörfer, 2003; Nowak et al., 2003; Witney et al., 2004) or used digital anesthesia (Nowak et al., 2001; Augurelle et al., 2003), and concluded that impaired cutaneous feedback increased the overall grip force, but did not affect the modulation of grip force in anticipation of load force.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on impaired cutaneous feedback.

claim: This study is the first to address the contribution of tactile information to grip force control in an intact motor system, using artificial cutaneous information.
source: Our study is the first to address this issue in an intact motor system, using artificial cutaneous information.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current study compared to previous research.

claim: Artificial skin-stretch increased the predictive grip force by increasing both the baseline grip force and the modulation in anticipation of the predicted load force.
source: Our results showed that artificial skin-stretch increased the predictive grip force by increasing both the baseline grip force and the modulation in anticipation of the predicted load force.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: The size of the effect of skin-stretch on grip force was linear with the amount of stretch.
source: In addition, we determined that the size of this effect was linear with the amount of stretch.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: The timescales of the evolution of the baseline grip force and modulation components were different – the baseline grip force increased immediately together with the perceptual illusion, and the modulation evolved gradually.
source: Interestingly, the timescales of the evolution of these two components were different – the baseline grip force increased immediately together with the perceptual illusion, and the modulation evolved gradually.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: Previous studies have determined that artificial skin-stretch causes an increase in the perceived load force.
source: Previous studies have determined that artificial skin-stretch causes an increase in the perceived load force (Gleeson et al., 2009; Matsui et al., 2013; Quek et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on skin-stretch and perceived load force.

claim: A similar increase in estimated load force can affect the predictive modulation of grip force.
source: One possibility is therefore that a similar increase in estimated load force can affect the predictive modulation.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed effects.

claim: The estimation of the force field stiffness could have been updated directly.
source: Alternatively, the estimation of the force field stiffness (Leib et al., 2016) could have been updated directly.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed effects, with a citation to previous work on stiffness estimation.

claim: The participants may have interpreted the additional tactile stimuli as indicative of a more slippery contact surface at the interface with the fingers.
source: Another possible explanation is that the participants may have interpreted the additional tactile stimuli as indicative of a more slippery contact surface at the interface with the fingers (Johansson and Westling, 1984; Flanagan and Wing, 1990), hence leading to an increase in the grip force which is entirely unrelated to the perceptual illusion of a harder object.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed effects, with citations to previous work on grip force and slipperiness.

claim: Previous studies showed that to reduce the risk of slippage, participants initially apply excessive grip force by applying a safety margin beyond the sufficient amount of grip force.
source: Previous studies have shown that to reduce the risk of slippage, participants initially apply excessive grip force by applying a safety margin beyond the sufficient amount of grip force.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: With repeated interactions with the environment, the baseline grip force lessens and adjusts to the expected load force.
